Her commitment to justice has set Iran’s authorities against her. They have thrown her in prison twice: once in 2010 and again in 2019. She remains in prison today. Nasrin is being held in Shahr-e Rey prison, a notorious women’s prison, where torture and mistreatment are rife. Will you donate £20 to Amnesty International UK Section Charitable Trust today? Your gift could help us Campaign for Nasrin’s freedom and help reunite her with her family. Right now, Amnesty International is working to protect human rights across the globe. We are committed to shining a light on injustice, and standing up for people who stand up for others — just like Nasrin. In Iran, women and girls above a certain age are required by law not to leave their homes unless they cover their hair, arms and legs. Women that don’t, face prison, flogging or a fine. In 2018, a movement against the forced veiling law erupted when one woman staged a solo act of resistance. She removed her headscarf and silently waved it on the end of a stick. Countless women across lran joined her, and became known as the ‘Girls of Revolution Street’. Nasrin defended some of these women in court, but was then herself arrested. By going after her, the lranian authorities are attacking women’s rights. All women should be free to choose what they wear, and lawyers should be free to defend their right to do so. A gift of £20 could help us publicise the facts of Nasrin’s case, to increase the pressure on the lranian authorities. After two grossly unjust trials, Nasrin now faces 148 lashes and 38 years in prison — the harshest sentence against a human rights defender in Iran for years. Charges against her include “inciting corruption and prostitution”. It’s part of a huge crackdown on free speech and dissent in Iran. More and more people like Nasrin are locked up, tortured, intimidated and more, just for speaking up for human rights. The authorities carry out floggings and have executed hundreds of people. During her release Nasrin tested positive for the coronavirus, which her husband says she caught in prison. RawCombinedText: ETHIOPIA EMERGENCY APPEAL MEDECINS SANS FRONTIERES DOCTORS WITHOUT BORDERS Albert Vifias, MSF emergency coordinator in Tigray, Ethiopia Hundreds of thousands of people have been -* forced to leave their homes in the Tigray region of northern Ethiopia after fighting broke out in November last year. MSF teams have been providing medical care to affected people since mid-December. Albert Viiias is MSF’s emergency coordinator in Tigray. “After several attempts, we finally entered the capital of Tigray, Mekele, more than a month after the violence started. The city was quiet. There was electricity, but no basic supplies. The local hospital was running at 30 to 40 per cent, with little medication. There were almost no patients, which is always a very bad sign. In Adigrat, the situation was very tense and the hospital was in a terrible condition. Most of the staff had left, there were hardly any medicines and no food and water. Some patients were malnourished. We supplied the hospital with medicines and bought emergency food in the markets that were still open. Together with the remaining staff, we cleaned the building and organised waste collection. Little by little we rehabilitated the hospital so that it could function. NO TELEPHONES Beyond the hospitals, around 80 or 90 per cent of the health centres we visited were not functional. One woman had been in labour for seven days without being able to give birth. Her life was saved because we Sint “<    - eae. MSF teams distribute essential items to families displaced by the fighting. Photograph © Ciaudia Blume/MSF were able to transport her to Mekele. I saw people arrive at hospital on bicycles carrying a patient from 30 km away. The impact of the violence is visible in the buildings and cars with bullet holes. RawCombinedText: YEMEN EMERGENCY APPEAL MSF anaesthetist Lenka Cervenova and her team care for a four-year-old boy after surgery in Dhi As-Sufal hospital in Yemen's Ibb province. Photograph © Majd Aljunaid/MSF ALISON CRIADO-PEREZ MSF NURSE The conflict in Yemen is now in its sixth year. In Marib, in central Yemen, nearly three million people have been displaced from their homes and are living in makeshift camps close to the frontline. Pregnant women and children are in desperate need of medical care. “When we arrived in Marib, we found the local hospitals overwhelmed by the sheer number of people and by an influx of war-wounded. Around 2.7 million people are in the province now, many of them displaced from their homes elsewhere and looking for a safe haven. People were living in makeshift shelters made of plastic and metal sheets. There were no latrines, just pits dug in the ground outside the tents. People were very worried about their health, about the risk of disease, about not having enough food. We were very concerned about the health of mothers and children, and pregnant women were a major worry too. Over the next month, our small team worked around the clock to set up clinics providing basic healthcare and to supply hospitals that were struggling. Getting medicines to this part of Yemen wasnt easy. Supplies often had to cross frontlines. One of our trucks carrying antibiotics, medicines and other supplies was hijacked. It was an incredibly difficult environment to work in. “As the frontline approaches Marib city, people sheltering in the area may find themselves with no place else to go.” Along with general healthcare, we provided routine vaccinations for children and offered antenatal and postnatal care. We saw a lot of pregnant women and children and were able to refer pregnant women with complications to larger hospitals for emergency caesareans. It made a real difference. The day we started working in a rural hospital near the frontline, a woman came in with a breech DONATE NOW Call: 0800 055 79 81 seven days a week Or search ‘MSF ALP to make an online donation delivery who was having real difficulty. Our midwife assisted and everything went well. But who knows what would have happened to that woman if the hospital wasnt there. A DESPERATE SITUATION Since I left, many more people have come to the area. But Marib is no longer a safe place to be. In recent weeks, the frontlines have moved into the province, causing large numbers of injuries and forcing thousands more people to flee their homes. As the frontline approaches Marib city, we are concerned that people sheltering in the area may find themselves with no place else to go. After six years of conflict, the situation is desperate. These people need our help now more than ever.” Charity Registration Number 1026588 rf        MEDECINS SANS FRONTIERES WHAT IS HAPPENING IN YEMEN? Yemen is in the midst of civil war. After six years of conflict, the medical and humanitarian situation in Yemen continues to deteriorate. Poverty is widespread, malnutrition is on the rise and people are confronted by the daily threat of violence. Pregnant women struggle to access medical care. infant and maternal mortality are on the rise as mothers and children bear the brunt of an increasingly brutal conflict. MSF teams are providing urgent medical care to people caught up in this crisis. We work in 12 hospitals and health centres and support more than 20 hospitals and health facilities across the country. We provide medical support in emergency rooms, maternity wards and outpatient departments, conduct surgeries, and run mobile clinics in rural towns and villages. The situation remains desperate. We need your help now more than ever. Thank you. During Christian Aid Week, will you make a stand for better futures? We have 7 days to make a huge stand with families like Rose's, and millions more people across Kenya whose lives are threatened daily by storms, flash floods and drought. Let's stand together against climate chaos. Let's work with communities to help build reliable water systems - and better futures. Low cost dams save lives. And help people stand stronger. Every drop of water that falls is precious. So there needs to be a simple, sustainable and ingenious way to successfully collect it. Earth dams do just that. And your gift today can help build them. It’s time for change. You can be part of building a hunger free future. Donate £25 and join our movement for change. Together, we can end the need for food banks and build a stronger society — one where no one goes hungry. Even before Covid-19 hit, need for food banks was growing and had reached record levels. It’s time to come together to build a better future. The challenge is big, and we need your help. Join us now and together, we can end the need for food banks. Violence in Ethiopia’s Tigray region has seen more than two million people forced to flee their homes since the conflict started in November 2020. Over 63,000 have fled into neighbouring Sudan, while those displaced inside Ethiopia include around 100,000 refugees from Eritrea. The region remains a tinderbox. There have been reports of hundreds of people killed, of atrocities, including forced military recruitment of men and boys, and of widespread sexual violence against women. Displaced families urgently need shelter. People have been sleeping in the open air, with no access to water or food. UNHCR teams on the ground are doing all they can to protect people, but with funds running desperately low, they urgently need your support. £159 could pay for a shelter kit. With the rainy season fast approaching, the shelter you help provide could be lifesaving. She has been wrenched apart from them, just for standing up for what’s right. Now she faces a brutal sentence of 148 lashes and 38 years in prison in Tehran. Nasrin is a human rights lawyer in Iran. It’s an incredibly risky job, but she has dedicated her life to defending the rights of others. Whether that means fighting to end the death penalty, or battling laws that punish women and girls unless they cover themselves in public. Her commitment to justice has set lran’s authorities against her. They have thrown her in prison twice: once in 2010 and again in 2019. She remains in prison today. Nasrin is being held in Shahr-e Rey prison, a notorious women’s prison, where torture and mistreatment are rife. Will you support Amnesty International UK Section Charitable Trust today with a monthly donation of £5? Your gift could help us campaign for Nasrin’s freedom and help reunite her with her family. Right now, Amnesty International is working to protect human rights across the globe. We are committed to shining a light on injustice, and standing up for people who stand up for others — just like Nasrin. In Iran, women and girls above a certain age are required by law not to leave their homes unless they cover their hair, arms and legs. Women who don’t, face prison, flogging or a fine. In 2018, a movement against the forced veiling law erupted when one woman staged a solo act of resistance. She removed her headscarf and silently waved it on the end of a stick. Countless women across Iran joined her, and became known as the ‘Girls of Revolution Street’. Nasrin defended some of these women in court, but was then herself arrested. By going after her, the lranian authorities are attacking women’s rights. All women should be free to choose what they wear, and lawyers should be free to defend their right to do so. A gift of £5 a month could help us publicise the facts of Nasrin’s case, to increase the pressure on the Iranian authorities. After two grossly unjust trials, Nasrin now faces 148 lashes and 38 years in prison — the harshest sentence against a human rights defender in Iran for years. Charges against her include “inciting corruption and prostitution”. It’s part of a huge crackdown on free speech and dissent in Iran. More and more people like Nasrin are locked up, tortured, intimidated and more, just for speaking up for human rights. The authorities carry out floggings and have executed hundreds of people. In January, she was diagnosed with a heart condition which makes her liable to angina and chest pain. It is made worse by stress or physical exertion. Her cardiologist said she should avoid being stressed and be held in well-ventilated spaces. We are now very worried for Nasrin’s health inside a dangerous, unhygienic and overcrowded prison. Nasrin is among the hundreds of wrongly imprisoned people in Iran. No one should spend a single day in prison for peacefully exercising their rights. Your gift today of £5 a month could help Amnesty International lobby governments around the world to intervene in cases like Nasrin’s. We know this works. With the help of people like you, Amnesty International has secured the release of lawyers, journalists and photographers the world over. Your gifts mean we can investigate abuse, hold people to account, and push decision-makers to take action in defence of human rights. But we've got through it by pulling together, by acting as a community even when we've been physically apart. Alzheimer’s Society has been supporting people living with dementia and their loved ones for over 40 years. And since March 2020 our vital services; providing advice, guidance and emotional support to people affected by dementia, have been needed like never before. Yemeni women and children need our help now more than ever.” ALISON CRIADO-PEREZ MSF NURSE The conflict in Yemen is now in its sixth year. In Marib, in central Yemen, nearly three million people have been displaced from their homes and are living in makeshift camps close to the frontline. Pregnant women and children are in desperate need of medical care. “When we arrived in Marib, we found the local © hospitals overwhelmed by the sheer number of people and by an influx of war-wounded. Nearly 3 million people are in the province now, many of them displaced from elsewhere. People were living in makeshift shelters made of plastic and metal sheets. There were no latrines, just pits dug in the ground. People were worried about their health, about the risk of disease, about not having enough food. We were very concerned about the health of mothers and children, and pregnant women were also a major worry. Over the next month, our small team worked around the clock to set up clinics providing basic healthcare and to supply hospitals that were struggling. Getting medicines to this part of ‘Pregnant women and children are in desperate need of medical care’ Yemen wasn't easy. Supplies often had to cross _ frontlines. One of our trucks carrying antibiotics, medicines and other supplies was hijacked. It was an incredibly difficult environment to work in. Along with general healthcare, we provided routine vaccinations for children and offered . antenatal and postnatal care. We saw a lot of _ pregnant women and children and were able to refer pregnant women with complications to larger hospitals for emergency caesareans. It made a real difference. The day we started working ina rural hospital near the frontline, a woman came in witha breech delivery who was having real difficulty. Our midwife assisted and everything went well. But who knows what would have happened if the hospital wasn’t there. AN URGENT SITUATION Since I left, many more people have come to the area. But Marib is no longer a safe place to be. In recent weeks, the frontlines have moved into the province, causing large numbers of injuries and forcing thousands more people to flee their homes. After six years of conflict, the situation is desperate. These people need our help now more than ever. the conflict in yemen is now in its sixth year in marib in central yemen nearly three million people have been displaced from their homes and are living in makeshift camps close to the frontline pregnant women and children are in desperate need of medical care when we arrived in marib we found the local hospitals overwhelmed by the sheer number of people and by an influx of war wounded nearly million people are in the province now many of them displaced from elsewhere people were living in makeshift shelters made of plastic and metal sheets there were no latrines just pits dug in the ground people were worried about their health about the risk of disease about not having enough food we were very concerned about the health of mothers and children and pregnant women were also a major worry over the next month our small team worked around the clock to set up clinics providing basic healthcare and to supply hospitals that were struggling getting medicines to this part of pregnant women and children are in desperate need of medical care yemen wasn t easy supplies often had to cross frontlines one of our trucks carrying antibiotics medicines and other supplies was hijacked it was an incredibly difficult environment to work in along with general healthcare we provided routine vaccinations for children and offered antenatal and postnatal care we saw a lot of This is the response of our lifetime. Dear reader, I'm sure you’ll agree that the recent news coverage from around the world has been bleak. My teams and are deeply concerned by what we're hearing from our colleagues across the global Red Cross movement, too. Today wanted to tell you about the new international fund we’ve launched, dedicated to supporting people overseas, and ask if you can help. Every year since 1999, extreme poverty levels globally have fallen — but that changed last year. The World Bank estimates that somewhere between 119-124 million people fell into extreme poverty last year. That’s 20 years of progress, of communities lifting themselves out of poverty, damaged by the pandemic. It’s clear to us that we need to act, now. We've set up a new international fund specifically to reach people whose lives have changed for the worse. Their reality is a stark contrast to ours here in the UK — because despite the pain of last year, our nation’s vaccine rollout is going well, and things are opening up. However, that’s not the case for millions of people worldwide. It’s far from it. That’s why we’re asking if you can support our new fund with a donation today. Take the communities we work with in Cox’s Bazar in Bangladesh, for example, who rely on busy trading to earn money and provide for their families. Worryingly, there’s been more than a 60% drop in income for people there, due to factors out of their control (travel restrictions, supply chain disruptions, and limited buyers in the market, to name a few). Our resilience project in Rakhine, Myanmar, has been running since 2017, and think it’s another example worth sharing with you. People face crises on top of crises — climate change and ongoing conflict has led to more frequent cyclones and floods, household providers losing livelihoods, displacement, and limited access to healthcare. People who were vulnerable before the pandemic are now in an even more fragile position, and our help has never been more critical. Communities like those in Rakhine need support that’s tailored to these intense, complex needs — that takes into account every dimension of each crisis they’re facing. And in the wake of coronavirus, our reports show that those groups’ income had dropped less than others who hadn’t had that vital training. Ultimately, they were more prepared for the worst. With your help, we can continue to make a real impact and strengthen our programmes around the world, to reach people whose lives depend on it. These are people who have no safety net, nothing to fall back on, no savings to see them through. People who may care for children or elderly relatives, who have no idea how they’ll get through the week, who need a lifeline more than ever right now. RawCombinedText: An open letter to Guardian readers The people of Yemen need your help. For more than six years, we’ve lived under the shadow of war. In some areas of the country we are seeing near famine conditions. Children, women and men could die from hunger. Yet, the fighting goes on. The current offensive in Marib, less than 100 miles from my home in Sana’a, has killed hundreds and forced tens of thousands to flee. The war affects everything. Public sector workers, such as teachers and police officers, haven’t been paid regularly since 2017. Electricity is 900% more expensive than in 2015. People have sold all their assets, but many are barely surviving. Tragically, some have taken their own lives. To me, they are just as much casualties of this war as people who die when their homes are hit. When the bombing starts, my wife and take the children to the safe room. We tell them the explosions are people playing with fireworks. We haven't suffered a direct hit yet, but many of my neighbours haven't been so lucky. When go for a walk, see displaced families living on the sidewalk and under bridges, with only cardboard and plastic sheeting to protect them. And then we have COVID-19, which has seen the international community cut aid to Yemen. It feels as if, while our people suffer, the world is looking the other way. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said recently: “Millions of Yemeni children, women and men desperately need aid to live. Cutting aid is a death sentence.” So yes, the situation is dire. But no, we will not give up. Famine is edging closer, but it’s not too late to help people. UNHCR has identified the most at risk families, and with your help today could provide them with an Emergency Payment of £143. The payment of £143 supports a family of six and is based on the cost of a ‘Survival Minimum Expenditure Basket’ of essentials such as food, water and medicine. For a family on the brink of famine, it could be the difference between life and death. Thank you.
